title: Standard Streams
concept: The standard streams stdin, stdout, and stderr are the default channels for console I/O

steps.title: Including stdio.h header
steps.explanation:
**`#include <stdio.h>`** -- Header for standard I/O functions.

Every C program automatically receives **3 data channels (streams)** from the OS when it starts.

steps.title: Starting main function
steps.explanation:
**`int main() {`** -- When the program starts, the OS automatically opens three streams: `stdin`, `stdout`, and `stderr`.

All three are **`FILE *` type pointers**.

steps.title: Writing to standard output (stdout)
steps.explanation: **`fprintf(stdout, "This uses stdout\n");`** -- `fprintf` writes a formatted string to a **specified stream**. The structure is `fprintf(stream, format_string, values...)`, with the first argument specifying the output destination.

steps.title: printf is a shortcut for stdout
steps.explanation:
**`printf("printf is a shortcut for fprintf(stdout, ...)
");`** -- The `printf(...)` we have been using is actually a **shortcut function** that internally calls `fprintf(stdout, ...)`. In other words, `printf("Hello
")` is identical to `fprintf(stdout, "Hello
")`.
steps.code: printf("printf is a shortcut for fprintf(stdout, ...)\n");
steps.stdout:
This uses stdout
printf is a shortcut for fprintf(stdout, ...)

steps.title: Writing to standard error (stderr)
steps.explanation: **`fprintf(stderr, "Error: Something went wrong!\n");`** -- This time we send a message to **`stderr` (standard error stream)** instead of `stdout`. By default `stderr` is also connected to the terminal, so visually it looks the same as `stdout`.

steps.title: Variable declaration and input prompt
steps.explanation: **`int n;`** and **`fprintf(stdout, "Enter a number: ");`** -- Declares an integer variable `n` for user input and prints a prompt. Since `n` is declared but not initialized, it contains a **garbage value**, shown as `???` in the visualization.

steps.title: Simulating input
steps.explanation: **`n = 5;`** -- In practice you would use `scanf("%d", &n);` to read from **`stdin`** (standard input connected to the keyboard), but here we assume the user entered `5`.

steps.title: Printing the input value
steps.explanation: **`fprintf(stdout, "You entered: %d\n", n);`** -- Displays the assigned value on screen via `stdout`. `%d` is replaced with the integer value `5` of `n`, printing `"You entered: 5"`.

steps.title: Program termination
steps.explanation: **`return 0;`** -- When the program terminates normally, the three standard streams are automatically closed and any data remaining in the `stdout` buffer is flushed.

quiz.question: When running ./app > log.txt in the terminal, what is displayed on screen?
quiz.explanation:
The `>` operator redirects only stdout to the file.
stderr still goes to the screen (terminal), so error messages can be seen immediately.

misconceptions.wrong: There is no reason to use fprintf when printf works fine.
misconceptions.correct: When you learn file I/O, `fprintf(file, ...)` becomes necessary, and distinguishing stdout/stderr is foundational for system programming.
misconceptions.why: Following the Unix philosophy (pipelines) requires stream separation.

keyTakeaway: stdin, stdout, and stderr are file pointers automatically opened at program start, serving as the communication channels with the OS.
